title: Getting Your AC Ready for Chennai Summer: A March Checklist
excerpt: By mid-April, Chennai is at 40°C and every AC service calendar in the city is full. Here is the March checklist that gets your unit through summer and keeps the bill honest.

sections.heading: Why March, Not May
paragraphs: Chennai does not ease into summer. By the second week of April, the city is holding at 38-40°C, every AC in the neighbourhood is running twelve hours a day, and service calendars across the city are full. Book in March and you choose your slot. Wait for the first heatwave and you join a queue behind everyone else who waited too.

There is a technical reason too. Your AC has just sat through the northeast monsoon. Damp air, dust, and coastal salt have had months to settle on the coils and inside the drain line. A March service catches the small problems damp weather breeds — mould in the blower, a sluggish drain, early coil corrosion — before summer heat turns them into breakdowns.
bullets: Book a full service in March, before April fills every calendar
Ask for a deep clean if the unit skipped its post-monsoon service
Test-run the AC for thirty minutes now, not on the first hot night
Check the stabilizer, plug point, and MCB while loads are still light
Set a repeating two-week reminder for filter cleaning

sections.heading: What a Proper Pre-Summer Service Covers
paragraphs: A basic split AC service starts from ₹499 and covers filter cleaning, coil dusting, a drain check, and a performance test. If your AC skipped its post-monsoon service, or if it sits near the coast where sea air eats aluminium fins, ask for a deep clean instead — from ₹799, the coils are jet-washed, the blower wheel is scrubbed, and the drain tray is flushed.

Ask the technician for readings, not reassurance. Coil temperature, gas pressure, and amperage draw tell you exactly how the unit is performing. A healthy 1.5-ton split should pull a closed room down noticeably within fifteen minutes. If pressure is low, fix the leak now rather than discovering it on a 40°C afternoon — a gas top-up starts from ₹1,499, and a full R32 recharge runs ₹2,500-3,500.
bullets: Indoor coil and blower wheel cleaned, not just wiped
Outdoor condenser jet-washed and bent fins straightened
Drain line flushed so condensate cannot back up into the room
Gas pressure and compressor amperage recorded on the invoice
Thermostat accuracy, swing, and remote functions tested

sections.heading: Filters: The Two-Week Rule for Chennai Dust
paragraphs: Chennai dust is relentless — road grit, construction fallout along OMR, fine sand riding the sea breeze. A clogged filter chokes airflow, forces the compressor to run longer, and can push your power bill up by 10-15%. In peak summer, in a road-facing or construction-adjacent home, clean the filters every two weeks. In quieter interiors, once a month is the floor, not the target.

The job takes ten minutes and needs no tools. Switch the AC off, lift the front panel, slide the mesh filters out, and rinse them under a tap — water aimed at the back side pushes dust out the way it came in. Shake them off, let them dry fully in shade, and slide them back. Wet filters refitted in a hurry invite mould.

sections.heading: Set 24-26°C and Let the Fan Do the Rest
paragraphs: The instinct on a 40°C day is to set 18°C and hope. It does not cool the room faster — it only makes the compressor run longer once the room is cold. Every degree you raise the set point saves roughly 6% on cooling power, which is why BEE made 24°C the default. Set 24-26°C, and over a Chennai summer of eight-hour daily runs, the difference shows up as real money on your EB bill.

Pair the AC with the ceiling fan on low. Moving air feels 2-3°C cooler on the skin, so a room set at 26°C feels close to 24°C without the compressor working for it. At night, use sleep mode or a timer — Chennai eases slightly after 2 a.m., and the AC does not need to fight as hard while you sleep.

sections.heading: Stabilizers, Voltage, and the Summer Grid
paragraphs: Chennai's grid works hardest on summer evenings, and voltage sags and spikes come with the territory — especially in older neighbourhoods and fast-growing suburbs. The most vulnerable part of your AC is its PCB, and PCB repairs run ₹1,499-4,999. A correctly rated stabilizer costs less than a single bad spike, and March is the month to check that yours still works.

Most inverter ACs tolerate a wide voltage band — many are rated for roughly 145-285V — so manufacturers often say a stabilizer is optional. Near the operating limits, though, protection circuits trip and cooling stops. For a 1.5-ton split, a 4 kVA stabilizer is the standard fit. While you are at it, have loose plug points and a warm-to-touch MCB looked at; weak contacts burn out in exactly the week you need the AC most.

sections.heading: Cut the Heat Before It Reaches the AC
paragraphs: Your AC's real enemy is the heat pouring into the room, and Chennai's west sun is brutal from 3 p.m. onward. Every watt of heat you block is a watt the compressor never has to remove. The cheapest cooling upgrades are not electrical at all — they are curtains, sealant, and a little discipline about doors.
bullets: Blackout or thick-weave curtains on west- and south-facing windows
Foam-tape the gaps around window frames and under doors
Shade the outdoor unit if you can, but never box it in
Keep balcony and bathroom doors closed while cooling
Move heat-throwing appliances out of the cooled room where possible

sections.heading: When an Old AC Costs More Than It Saves
paragraphs: There is a point where loyalty to an old unit becomes expensive. A ten-year-old 3-star fixed-speed AC can draw 30-40% more power than a new 5-star inverter for the same cooling. On heavy Chennai summer usage, that efficiency gap alone can add several thousand rupees to a season's bills — before you count a single repair.

Use three signals. Two gas top-ups within a year means a leak that cleaning will not cure. Compressor work — from ₹4,999 on an ageing unit — rarely makes sense past year ten. And when any single repair estimate crosses roughly 40% of a comparable new unit's price, put the money toward the new unit instead. An honest technician will tell you which side of the line you are on; ask for the numbers.

takeaways: Service in March from ₹499 — before the April rush, not after the first breakdown.
Clean filters every two weeks in dusty areas; a clogged filter can add 10-15% to the bill.
Run at 24-26°C with the ceiling fan on; each degree higher saves roughly 6%.
A 4 kVA stabilizer for a 1.5-ton split costs less than one PCB repair.
Two gas refills in a year, or a repair above 40% of a new unit's price, means replace.

faqs.question: Is one service a year enough for a Chennai AC?
faqs.answer: For most Chennai homes, two services a year work best — one in March before the heat, one after the northeast monsoon. The city's dust, humidity, and coastal air are harder on ACs than in most of India. An AMC from ₹1,199 per unit per year typically covers this schedule without you tracking dates.

faqs.question: Do inverter ACs really need a stabilizer in Chennai?
faqs.answer: Most modern inverter units are rated for wide voltage bands, often around 145-285V, so they ride out routine fluctuations. Summer-evening sags and spikes near those limits can still trip protection circuits or stress the PCB. A correctly rated stabilizer — about 4 kVA for a 1.5-ton split — remains cheap insurance.

faqs.question: My AC cools fine, but bills have jumped. What should I check?
faqs.answer: A sudden jump usually points to clogged filters, dirty coils, or marginally low gas — all caught by a standard service from ₹499. If bills stay high after a proper clean and gas check, the unit itself may be the problem, especially past eight to ten years. Ask for pressure and amperage readings so the decision rests on numbers.

meta.title: Chennai Summer AC Checklist: Service Before the April Rush
meta.description: Service before the April rush, filters every two weeks, 24-26°C settings, stabilizer checks, and when to replace an old AC — a Chennai owner's March checklist.
